scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The ballo emerged during the Italian Quattrocento as a sophisticated Renaissance dance form.
Fifteenth-century dance masters Domenico da Piacenza and Guglielmo Ebreo da Pesaro composed numerous balli and authored foundational treatises containing choreography and theoretical principles.

By the Baroque period, the form expanded significantly, incorporating vocal numbers in works by Claudio Monteverdi and Francesco Lambardi, and instrumental interludes by composers such as George Frideric Handel.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Considered a vital branch of gymnastics and a study in personal elegance, the ballo was designed to bestow a gracious presence, fine posture, and smooth gait while banishing clumsiness.
It was practiced during civic celebrations, courtly festivities, and elite social gatherings, though masters cautioned against the moral hazards of human vanity in such settings.
Today it is a historical tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music for the fifteenth-century ballo was structured around four distinct misure: the slow bassadanza, the quadernaria (one-sixth faster), the saltarello (two-sixths faster), and the piva (twice as fast).
Later Baroque iterations incorporated lute tablatures, soprano voice scores, two recorders, and violins as seen in Handel's revisions of Il pastor fido.
Listen for the lute, recorders, violin.
The pulse is variable across four misure (bassadanza structured as slow 64 or 32; quadernaria, saltarello, and piva at faster relative fractions).

Characterized by frequent shifts in tempo and meter, moving fluidly from a slow foundational bassadanza pulse to brisk saltarello and piva rhythms, accompanied by plucked strings and melodic wind instruments.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historical figures include Domenico da Piacenza, Guglielmo Ebreo da Pesaro, Fabritio Caroso da Sermoneta, Claudio Monteverdi, Francesco Lambardi, Giambattista Dufort, and George Frideric Handel.

Treatises distinguish between Italian, French, and Spanish styles of balli and balletti, noting shifts in foot positions and stylistic preferences across European courts, particularly as French theatrical dance gained prominence in the early eighteenth century.
The ballo shares lineage with the medieval basse danse and influenced later theatrical ballet, the tarantella, and various Baroque balletti forms.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Ballo is parent of Bassadanza: Serves as the primary slow tempo measure underpinning many early balli.
Ballo is variant of Saltarello: Employed as a faster tempo measure (two-sixths faster than the bassadanza) within ballo compositions.
Ballo is child of Ballet: Evolved from Renaissance court balli and Italian-French theatrical dance developments.
